intro: Silton is a small village near Gillingham in north Dorset, and in the field behind its church of St Nicholas stands Wyndham's Oak, said to be up to 1,000 years old and the oldest tree in Dorset. It is named after Sir Hugh Wyndham, a 17th-century judge who owned the manor and is said to have sat in its shade. A footpath from the churchyard leads to it.

trees.story:
When it was measured in April 2008, the trunk of this oak was 12 metres round, about the width of a small room, and the hollow bole stood almost 8 metres high. It is said to be up to 1,000 years old and the oldest tree in Dorset, which is what the reader who sent it to us called it too.

It is named after Sir Hugh Wyndham, a judge of the Common Pleas who bought the manor of Silton soon after 1660 and is said to have sat in its shade while he thought over his cases. Darker stories cling to it as well. It was reputedly used as a gallows for rebels convicted after the Monmouth Rebellion of 1685. Long before either, it was one of the oaks that marked the boundary between Selwood Forest and the royal hunting forest of Gillingham.

It was engraved in the reign of George III, and in 2018 it was one of ten trees in the Woodland Trust's vote for England's Tree of the Year.

Today it stands in a meadow on a private farm just behind St Nicholas' church, where a memorial to the judge hangs inside. The local walking route reaches it on a footpath and leaves by a gate beside the churchyard wall.
trees.how_to_recognise: A huge, low-domed oak alone in the meadow behind St Nicholas' churchyard, its short, grey, hollow trunk swollen and fissured beneath a broad green crown.

question_meta: Wyndham's Oak in Silton, Dorset: how old it is, why it is named after a judge, and how to walk to it.
question_answer: Wyndham's Oak is a pedunculate oak in a field behind St Nicholas' church in Silton, near Gillingham in Dorset. It is said to be up to 1,000 years old and the oldest tree in Dorset, and in 2008 its trunk measured 12 metres round. A footpath from the churchyard reaches it.
question_context: The oak takes its name from Sir Hugh Wyndham, a judge of the Common Pleas who bought the manor of Silton soon after 1660 and is said to have sat in its shade to consider his cases. Tradition also says rebels convicted after the Monmouth Rebellion were hanged from it. It was one of the oaks that marked the boundary between Selwood Forest and the royal forest of Gillingham. In April 2008 its hollow trunk measured 12 metres in circumference, with a bole almost 8 metres high. It was engraved in the reign of George III and was one of ten candidates for England's Tree of the Year in 2018. It stands on a privately owned farm, reached by a footpath from the churchyard of St Nicholas. Its hollow trunk, swollen and fissured, now carries a broad, rounded crown that is still green every summer. A memorial to Sir Hugh Wyndham is inside the church, and Gillingham's local walking route passes the oak.
